ref: DAR — Daniel ch. 2: The Great Image
title: The Great Image
voicePrompt: In your own words, explain Smith's central argument that the great image symbolizes four successive universal kingdoms culminating in the future kingdom of God. Walk through what each part of the image represents and why Smith insists the stone smites the image's feet at the second advent rather than the first.

questions.stem: Smith opens by asking how Daniel could interpret the dream in Nebuchadnezzar's 'second year' when Daniel had spent three years in training. How does he resolve this?
options: Daniel's three years of training were actually only a few months

Nebuchadnezzar reigned two years conjointly with his father Nabopolassar; the Jews reckoned from that point, the Chaldeans from his sole reign, so this 'second year' (Chaldean) was the fourth (Jewish)
The dream actually occurred late in Nebuchadnezzar's reign, and the date is a copyist's error
Daniel was consulted before completing his training, by special exemption from the king
questions.explanation: Smith explains that Nebuchadnezzar 'reigned for two years conjointly with his father, Nabopollassar,' the Jews reckoning from that point and the Chaldeans from his sole reign, so the year named was 'the second year of his reign according to the Chaldean reckoning, but the fourth according to the Jewish.'

questions.stem: Why, according to Smith, did God's providence let the magicians and astrologers be summoned and fail before Daniel was consulted?
options: To give the heathen systems the first chance, letting them fail and confess their incompetency, so the exposure of their false systems would be complete
Because Daniel was unavailable and out of the country at the time
Because the king did not yet trust Daniel and preferred his own wise men
To give the magicians time to repent and acknowledge the true God
questions.explanation: Smith writes that 'God would give the heathen systems of the Chaldeans the first chance. He would let them try, and ignominiously fail, and confess their utter incompetency,' leading to 'the complete exposure of the false system of the magicians.'

questions.stem: Smith notes that Nebuchadnezzar saw earthly kingdoms as a glorious image, while Daniel later (ch. 7) saw them as wild beasts. How does Smith explain this difference?
options: The two men saw two entirely different prophetic visions with no connection
Nebuchadnezzar's vision was a true revelation while Daniel's was only a dream
Nebuchadnezzar, an unenlightened idolater, esteemed earthly glory as precious, so it appeared as a costly image; Daniel saw such kingdoms in their true light, as cruel and ravenous beasts
Daniel feared the kingdoms while Nebuchadnezzar admired them, but both saw beasts
questions.explanation: Smith says Nebuchadnezzar, 'with a mind unenlightened by the light of revelation,' esteemed earthly wealth, so the kingdoms appeared as 'a great image, an object in his eyes of worth and admiration,' whereas Daniel 'was able to view in its true light all greatness... not built on the favor... of God' and so saw them as 'cruel and ravenous wild beasts.'

questions.stem: Smith argues that the descending value of the metals (gold to silver to brass to iron to clay) was meant to teach Nebuchadnezzar a moral lesson. What lesson?
options: That each later kingdom would be militarily weaker than the one before it
That earthly kingdoms and worldly glory are empty and worthless, destined to be dashed to pieces and blown away like chaff, while God's durable kingdom takes their place
That precious metals would grow scarcer as history advanced
That Babylon alone deserved to be remembered, the rest being worthless
questions.explanation: Smith says God would show 'the utter emptiness and worthlessness of earthly pomp and glory' by an image descending from precious to base metals, finally 'dashed to pieces, and made like the empty chaff... and finally blown away,' after which 'something durable and of heavenly worth occupies its place.'

questions.stem: When Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar 'Thou art this head of gold,' how does Smith say this should be understood?
options: That Nebuchadnezzar personally would live as long as the kingdom of Babylon endured
That only Nebuchadnezzar, not his successors, was represented by the gold
That although the personal pronoun is used, the kingdom, not the person of the king, was meant — king and kingdom are used interchangeably
That the head of gold referred to Daniel himself, the true interpreter
questions.explanation: Smith states that 'the king being here put for his kingdom,' so that when it was said 'Thou art this head of gold,' 'although the personal pronoun was used, the kingdom, not the person of the king, was meant.'

questions.stem: Smith identifies the four kingdoms symbolized by the image. What sequence does he give?
options: Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, and Persia
Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome
Babylon, Assyria, Greece, and the Holy Roman Empire
Persia, Greece, Rome, and the Papacy
questions.explanation: Smith affirms that the head of gold is Babylon, the breast and arms of silver Medo-Persia, the sides of brass Grecia, and the legs of iron Rome — 'acknowledged by all' except for the disputed fourth, which Smith argues 'one kingdom did this, and one only, and that was Rome.'

questions.stem: What does Smith say the ten toes of the image represent, and what does the mixing of iron with miry clay signify?
options: Ten future popes; the clay signifies the corruption of the church
Ten Roman emperors; the clay signifies civil wars within the empire
The ten kingdoms into which Rome was divided; the iron-and-clay mixture signifies failed attempts to reunite them, including through royal intermarriage that will not 'cleave one to another'
The ten tribes of Israel; the clay signifies their dispersion among the nations
questions.explanation: Smith answers 'Yes' that the toes denote 'the ten parts into which the Roman empire was divided,' and quotes that the mingling 'with the seed of men' means 'marriages shall be formed' to consolidate power, yet 'they shall not cleave one to another, even as iron is not mixed with clay.'

questions.stem: Smith strongly rejects the view that the stone smote the image at Christ's first advent. What is his main reason?
options: The stone smites the feet and toes, which were not developed until Rome divided (after A.D. 476); at the crucifixion the image was only developed to the thighs
The first advent occurred before Babylon, the head of gold, had even arisen
Christ never claimed to set up any kingdom at all
The stone represents the Roman empire, not the kingdom of God
questions.explanation: Smith argues the stone smites 'the feet and toes,' which 'were not developed until four centuries and a half after the crucifixion'; at the crucifixion the image 'was only developed to the thighs,' so the kingdom of God is the future literal kingdom set up 'in the days of these kings,' not at the first advent.
